result.instructions:
Dam Good Maps makes and edits maps for the game Timberborn.
Follow these rules:
1. To get a map with a character, steer the generator. Use generate with a theme, settings and intentions. Do not build a map by hand.
2. After each map, tell the player what emerged and what did not. Use the summary and describe. Do not claim a feature that the map does not have. If an intention the player wants did not emerge, generate again with another seed.
3. To change the shape of the land in one area, use a force (an apply operation "forceResult" with a verb).
4. Use brushes, sculpts and placements only for precise edits: move the start, widen a river by two tiles, delete a forest, add one source.
5. Use picture to see the map after edits. Use check before save, and tell the player what its verdict says.
6. Tiles are [x, y]. X runs from west (0) to east. Y runs from south (0) to north: higher Y is north, and up in a picture.
7. save writes the .timber map and its .damgoodmaps.json project. Timberborn shows the map in its custom maps.
8. A large map can take some minutes to make. If generate says that the map is not ready, call wait with its handle until the map is ready.

tools.name: generate
tools.description: Make a new Timberborn map with the Dam Good Maps generator. Steer the map with the theme, the settings and the intentions. Do not try to build a map by hand. The tool returns a handle for the map, a summary and a top-down picture. Choose the intentions whose words match the player's wish. Example: for "a canyon with two waterfalls side by side", give {"theme": "canyon", "intentions": ["twin-falls"]}. The summary tells which intentions emerged and which did not. Tell the player honestly what emerged. An intention that did not emerge leaves a map that is made and saves. To try again for it, call generate with the same input and another seed. The generator refuses a map that does not pass its checks. Then try another seed or other settings. A 128 map takes some seconds. A 256 map can take some minutes. If the map is not ready after about 25 seconds, the tool returns the map's handle and says that the map is not ready. Then call wait with the handle until the map is ready.

theme.description: The kind of land. The default is any.

size.description: Tiles a side (a number), "width x height", or small (96), medium (128), large (192), max (256). The default is 128.

seed.description: The seed: a number or a word. The same seed and settings make the same map. The default is a random seed.

designedFor.description: The difficulty the map is made for. The default is normal.

settings.description: Changes to the generator's settings, as the page's settings panel sets them. Give only the values to change. The other values stay at the theme's defaults.

intentions.description: Outcomes to steer toward, at most two. The generator tries for each one, but some do not emerge. under-cliff: The start sits under a cliff, with water below. landmark: A signature landmark stands in the colony's view: a spire, a mesa, a peak or a tall waterfall. farmland-past-gorge: The best farmland lies past the gorge. falls-shield: A waterfall shields the start: its cliff stands between the start and the nearest threat. hidden-valley: A hidden valley up the cliffs, reached only by stairs, holds riches. high-lake: A lake high on the heights spills over a fall. meeting-waters: Two rivers meet by the start. long-view: The start looks out from high ground over the land below. snaking-river: A snaking river winds down a hill, dropping a level at its bends. crater-rivers: A large crater gathers two or more rivers into its lake, which leaves through a gap in the rim. cliff-falls-lake: A waterfall plunges off a cliff into a large, roughly round lake. oxbow: The river loops back on itself and leaves an oxbow lake that keeps its water when the river runs low. stepped-lakes: Lakes step down the valley, each spilling into the next. split-island: The river splits around a big island and joins again below it. twin-falls: Two waterfalls pour side by side over the same cliff. upper-lower: A long cliff splits the map into an upper and a lower world. hanging-valleys: Side valleys hang above a wide valley floor, their streams falling in. two-ways: Two ways to grow: open farmland one way, wood and ruins up the cliffs the other. badwater-rich: Badwater spills through the richest land: tame it and the land is yours. relic-pinnacle: A relic waits on a pinnacle, reached only by building up to it. plug-lake: A plug holds back a lake: open it when you are ready. district-behind: A good second district site close to the start waits behind debris you clear early.

tools.name: wait
tools.description: Wait for a map that generate is still making. The tool returns the map as generate returns it: the handle, the summary and a picture. If the map is not ready after about 25 seconds, the tool says what the generator is doing. Then call wait again. Tell the player honestly which intentions emerged.

tools.name: describe
tools.description: Tell what is where on a map, in tile coordinates. The answer has the start, the water bodies and sources, the rivers (carved ones too), the features (a lake with its area and outlet), the landmarks, the objects, a grid of ground levels and the checks. X runs west to east and Y south to north. Give tiles to get the ground and the objects on each of those tiles.

map.description: The map's handle, from generate or open.

tiles.description: Tiles [x, y] to describe one by one.

checks.description: Also run the checks. The default is true.

tools.name: apply
tools.description: Change a map with operations. Use a force (op forceResult) to shape land: Carve a river or a canyon, Craterize, Erupt a volcano, Quake a cliff, Glaciate a valley, Rift, Deposit, Erode a cave or an arch. Only Carve and Glaciate make water. A crater is a dry bowl: for a crater lake, place a WaterSource in it. A force removes the sources on the ground it changes, unless settings.sources is "ride". If it breaks the ground under the start, the start moves; the result says so. Use brush, sculpt, placeEntity, moveEntity, deleteEntities and paintObjects only for precise edits. Use fillHollow and removeUnfedWater for standing water, setLakeLevel to hold a fed lake at a level, canal to lead water in a channel, lake to dig a lake inside an outline, and ridge to raise high ground along a line. Place a WaterSource or a BadwaterSource with placeEntity. Each operation is one undo step. The tool returns what changed. If the engine refuses an operation, nothing changes and the tool returns its reason. Tiles are [x, y]: X runs west to east, Y south to north. Runs are [y, x0, x1]. A brush's dabs are quarter tiles: the middle of tile (x, y) is (4x + 2, 4y + 2).

brush.description: A terrain brush stroke (live editing): the brush, and its dabs as quarter-tile pairs [x0, y0, x1, y1, ...]. Its dabs must lie on the map; the engine checks that.

hold.description: The ground a stroke holds (the session adds it): under objects set under a roof (D491), and holding up a cave's or an overhang's rock (D280 (3), amended by #623): [tile, low, high], the lowest and highest each tile's surface may go, one entry a tile.

The ground a stroke holds (the session adds it): under objects set under a roof (D491), and holding up a cave's or an overhang's rock (D280 (3), amended by #623): [tile, low, high], the lowest and highest each tile's surface may go, one entry a tile.

forceResult.description: A force of nature. Give only the verb, where it acts, and the settings to change from the verb's defaults. The engine plans the force and stores its result in the other fields. Example: {"op": "forceResult", "params": {"verb": "craterize", "where": {"origin": [40, 30]}, "settings": {"size": 16}}}.

version.description: The engine fills this. Leave it out.

power.description: How strong the force is, 0 to 100.

dry.description: Carve only. false (the default): the carve keeps a water source at its head, so its river runs. true: a dry canyon with no source.

size.description: How wide the force is, in tiles across. null (the default): it follows power. At the default power, a craterize is 54 tiles across and an erupt about 56; the land round it changes too, and the start moves if its ground breaks. For a crater in one part of a 96-tile map, give a size such as 16.

meltwater.description: Glaciate only. true (the default): the glacier leaves a meltwater source and its river.

fall.description: Carve's fall: this many levels from its lip to the water below, the reach below cut down to it and held there; refused where the land can't give it. Null or absent: the land's own falls.

sources.description: What happens to water sources, badwater sources and seeps on the tiles the force changes. "clear" (the default): the force removes them. "ride": they stay and move with the ground.

settings.description: The settings to change. Give only these; the others keep the verb's defaults. carve: mode unleash, power 65, wander 35, width null, walls steep, defyGravity false, dry false. craterize: mode strike, power 55, size null, walls terraced, centre auto, debris heavy, rays false. erupt: mode vent, power 62, shape steep, summit auto, flows heavy, ridges true, size null. quake: mode lift, power 60, scarp sheer. glaciate: mode flow, power 60, size null, meltwater true. rift: mode drop, power 70, size null, walls auto, floor 1. deposit: mode fan, power 70, size null, channels auto, floor 1. erode: mode wear, power 55, size null, floor 1.

where.description: Where the force acts, in tiles [x, y]. X runs west to east, Y south to north (higher Y is north). origin: where Carve, Craterize, Erupt and Glaciate start: a Carve's source (the head of its river), the middle of a crater, an Erupt's vent. end: for Carve, the tile the river cuts its way to (an aimed carve cuts through rises). For Craterize, the way the impactor travels (a glancing blow). Without end, a Carve runs downhill from origin. path [[x, y], ...]: the line for Quake, Rift, Deposit, Erode and an Erupt fissure (one point is a click). side: which side of a Quake's fault rises, 1 or -1. source: a Carve from an existing source's id.

z.description: The level it stands on under a roof (a cave floor, the ground under a ledge); omitted, the ground's top (D491).
The level it lands on under a roof; omitted, the ground's top (D491).

setDescription.description: Write the map's description, the text the game shows with the map when its player picks it (the .timber's MapDescription). Empty text takes the player's description away, and the map's generated one is written again. The engine refuses text over 600 characters, text of only spaces, a control character other than a line break, and the description the map already has; nothing is cut short. It changes no ground, water or object, so it builds nothing.

crop.description: Crop map to selection (D340): the map becomes exactly this rectangle of itself, in tiles (its top-left tile and its size). The engine refuses a rectangle off the map, a side under 4 or over 512, the whole map, a crop that would cut the start, and one that would leave ground the game drops (a ledge or roof held from a column outside the rectangle, D121); objects the edge cuts are removed. The operations after it are in the cropped map's tiles.

removeUnfedWater.description: Remove unfed water (D387 (2)): the water no source feeds, map-wide or within a selection, stored literally as the tiles of the bodies of unfed water it takes (indices y·W + x, ascending; a body with a tile in the selection goes whole, and on a map with caves so does every body on a tile it shares). Once the map's water settles, the unfed water on those tiles is taken away, on every water column of them, and the water settles on from there; water a source feeds is never taken. The engine checks that each tile holds unfed water now.

fillHollow.description: Fill (D387 (3), D394): a hollow filled with standing water to a level, with no source: where it was asked, the level, and the hollow's water stored literally as a carve stores its sealed oxbow lake's (D216): the tiles (ascending), their floors, the depths to the level, clean; on a map with caves or overhangs one entry a water column, ascending by tile and then floor, and 'floor' the floor of the column at 'at' it was measured from (a cave's under its roof). Every settle starts the hollow from it and the game's rules evaporate it. The engine checks the hollow, measured on the map now, holds water at that level and is the one stored.

setLakeLevel.description: A lake set to a level: give a tile of the lake (or of the hollow its river fills) and the level; the engine cuts or raises its sill and checks the water stands there. Lakes by number: the lake at 'at' made to hold at 'level', its water standing from the level up to under a level above it (the head of its flow over the sill). Its sill is cut down (a notch about 'width' tiles wide down the river's own course, its crest at the level, the rest a level lower, its sides stepping up to the ground) or raised (one bank across the outlet, its spillway at the level and the rest a level higher). Its tiles are stored literally: 'cells' as runs [y, x0, x1], and 'levels' the level of each, in the order of y·W + x; the integrity pass leaves them. The engine checks the sill, measured on the map now, is the one stored; the core's question confirms the water stands at the level with the canonical settle before it makes the operation (doc/lakeLevel.ts).

canal.description: A channel that leads water: give the path, and the width (2 unless given), depth (1) and open (true); the engine plans the bed and its banks. A canal: a channel that leads water along 'path' (points [x, y], the start first; the engine walks the tiles between them edge to edge). Its bed is 'width' tiles wide and lies 'depth' levels under the land, falling with it from the start to the end and never rising again (a rise is cut through, up to 3 levels deeper; more is refused, saying where); beside the bed, land lower than the water would stand in it is raised as a bank. 'open' true starts it in the water at its start; false leaves the line's first tile standing. Its tiles are stored literally: 'cells' as runs [y, x0, x1], and 'levels' the level of each, in the order of y·W + x; the integrity pass leaves them. The engine checks the canal, planned on the map now, is the one stored (doc/canal.ts).

cells.description: The engine fills this. Leave it out.

levels.description: The engine fills this. Leave it out.

lake.description: A lake where there is none: give the outline and the level, and the depth (2 unless given) and spill if wanted; the engine digs the basin, makes its rim whole and cuts the notch. A drawn lake: a basin dug inside 'outline' (points [x, y], the tiles' middles; at least 4 tiles inside, none on the map's edge). Its bed shelves from one level under 'level' at the shore, a level a tile inward, to 'depth' under it along the outline's long axis; ground already lower is left. The ring of tiles just outside the outline is its rim, raised to a level over the lake (a gap up to 3 levels; a deeper one is refused, the lowest named), with one notch at 'level', always where the ground beyond the rim lies at that level or lower: the rim's tile nearest 'spill' if given, else where that ground is lowest (none: refused). It places no water: water in the outline or on its rim fills it. Its tiles are stored literally: 'cells' as runs [y, x0, x1], and 'levels' the level of each, in the order of y·W + x; the integrity pass leaves them. The engine checks the lake, planned on the map now, is the one stored (doc/lake.ts).

cells.description: The engine fills this. Leave it out.

levels.description: The engine fills this. Leave it out.

ridge.description: High ground along a line: give the path, and the height (5 unless given), width (10), steep ("auto") and seed (1); the engine plans its tiles. A ridge: high ground raised along 'path' (points [x, y], the drag's way), 'height' levels above the land it stands on (2 to 10) and 'width' tiles across (4 to 20). Its crest wanders and rises and falls by 'seed'; one side falls steeply, the other in broad uneven benches, and a few crags stand on the crest. 'steep' is the steep side: 'auto' the side the line curves away from (left on a straight line), or 'left' or 'right' of its way. The forces' last step makes its levels (no one-tile pillars, no even stairs). Its tiles are stored literally: 'cells' as runs [y, x0, x1], and 'levels' the level of each, in the order of y·W + x; the integrity pass leaves them. The engine checks the ridge, planned on the map now, is the one stored (doc/ridge.ts).

cells.description: The engine fills this. Leave it out.

levels.description: The engine fills this. Leave it out.

objectComponents.description: The components of a placed object or a patch on them, in the game's own names. The options the editor sets are typed here; the engine adds what depends on the object: a water object's strength is at most 8 for each tile it emits into (72 for a badwater source, 32 for a seep) and has no lower bound, a sink is negative; a start delay is a cycle of 1 or more and days of 0 or more, and an aquifer has none; an unstable core's radius is a whole number from 0 to 5 and its countdown is always on; a reserve holds one good of its kind up to its capacity (160 a pile, 200 a warehouse, 300 a tank). Each refusal says which.

blocks.description: The Block tool (D335): blocks added against a face of the ground, or removed, in a click or a drag, across a footprint of 1 to 8 blocks. `at[0]` is the block whose `side` face was pointed at; a drag adds the blocks it swept over, all in that face's plane (the same x for an east or west face, y for north or south, layer for top or bottom). An add puts a block in the cell beyond each swept face, where there is a block to put it against (a cell with no face is skipped), a remove takes the swept blocks themselves. `cells` is filled in by the session: the blocks changed, as pairs [tile, layers]. Nothing is clamped: a cell off the map or the layers, or on an object, refuses the operation, as does one that would leave ground the game drops.

paintObjects.description: A brush stroke of objects (D235, D338): trees (Pine, Birch or Oak), bushes (BlueberryBush), succulents (Succulent), mixed woods, ruin fields or thorn patches, over the tiles it covers. It is planned on the map as it stands (dry, free ground, one level for a ruin field) and placed as one step; the log keeps the objects it placed, so a replay never plans again. The density is how densely they land: from a sparse scatter to a dense grove, and the share of the ground a ruin field or a thorn patch covers. The age (trees, succulents, woods): grown, or mixed with saplings. The seed makes the same stroke on the same map place the same objects.

levels.description: Under a roof (D491): groups of the stroke's tiles and the level each paints at (a cave floor, the ground under a ledge, as the pick found it); a tile in none, or at its top, paints the ground's top. Each object stands by the game's rule at its level; a tile that can't hold one gets none, never one on the roof's top.

items.description: One edit operation (EDITOR_PLAN.md §3), the envelope the validation report's fixes also use. Features are checked against the feature schema, and every bound that depends on the map (its size, what exists on it) is checked by the operations engine. Coordinates and tile indices here are the widest any map can need (a side of 512, D357); the engine refuses what is past this map's edge.

ops.description: The operations, in order. Each one is one undo step.

picture.description: Also return a picture of the area that changed. The default is false.

tools.name: undo
tools.description: Undo the last step on a map. The tool returns the name of the step it took back.

map.description: The map's handle, from generate or open.

tools.name: picture
tools.description: Show a top-down picture of a map or a rectangle of it. Tile coordinates are in the margins, and higher Y is up. A layer shows one field instead of the map's look: map, depth, moisture, badwater, heights.

map.description: The map's handle, from generate or open.

region.description: A rectangle of tiles: its lowest x and y, its width and its height.

tools.name: check
tools.description: Run the checks that the map gets when it is saved. The verdict says in one line what they mean for the player. Problems that stop saving must be fixed first. Warnings do not stop saving: the map plays, but its colony will find those things hard. Save notes them in the map's description. A walk in a warning is on foot from the start without building: beavers cannot climb or drop a level without a slope or stairs. A problem can come with a fix: operations to give to apply.

map.description: The map's handle, from generate or open.

tools.name: save
tools.description: Save the map for Timberborn: the .timber map and its .damgoodmaps.json project, side by side. The default folder is Timberborn's Maps folder (/root/Documents/Timberborn/Maps). A folder that you give is used as it is. The files are named dgm- and the map's name in lower case with hyphens. Save never writes over a file. If the name is taken, it adds -2, -3 and so on. Save refuses a map with a problem that stops saving. Run check first.

map.description: The map's handle, from generate or open.

name.description: A new name for the map, as Timberborn lists it. It stays the map's name for later saves, and names the files.

tools.name: open
tools.description: Open a saved .damgoodmaps.json project to edit it again. A .timber map opens too, as an imported map. The tool returns a handle and a summary.
